The Craft of Practitioner Voice

Practitioner Voice is not a tone. It is a discipline: start with the claim, stay visible, ground authority in consequence, compress without losing meaning, and leave real tension live. The goal is not to sound more personal. The goal is to make earned judgment useful to readers who have lived the problem.

The category existed before it had a name. Practitioners have been writing this way for years, on Substack, on martinfowler.com, in Cutter journals, in the margins of conference papers, and finding their way to it by instinct or luck. A good editor. An encouraging colleague. Someone who said: let your voice out. Without the category there were no guidelines. Without guidelines practitioners defaulted to the two models they knew: academic scaffolding or thought leadership polish. This piece is the beginning of guidelines that should have existed.

How to use AI without losing your voice

A year ago, I started thinking of it as alternative intelligence rather than artificial intelligence. Intelligence without consciousness: a different kind of mind, not a lesser one. That reframe matters for how you work with it.

How writers use AI, and what they owe their readers about it, is still unsettled. Two practitioners I respect have landed in opposite places.

Mik Kersten writes: “I decided to write every word in this book and did not use AI for any of the ideating, outlining, or writing. The writing process helped me slow down and contemplate, and I hope the process of reading this book will do the same for you.” The writing process itself is the point. AI would have short-circuited it. Mik’s approach would please William Zinsser, who wrote: “Writing is a form of thinking, whatever the subject.” AI makes it possible to produce without learning. That’s the trap.

Jurgen Appelo takes the opposite position. He wrote with a team of one human and multiple AI agents: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others. Some sections originated with him; others started with the agents and he refined them. His argument: creativity has always been collaborative. AI is the latest in a long lineage of tools that amplify human capacity. What matters is the experience the reader gets, not who or what generated each sentence.

Both positions are principled. I landed somewhere else.

Parkinson’s changed my cognitive processing. Not all at once. A word that used to surface instantly now takes a beat longer. A thread of argument that once held itself in working memory needs an external anchor. Sixty years of consequence-bearing experience didn’t disappear. The pattern recognition I built across careers in software development, management consulting, and organizational leadership stayed. What changed was the biological system I’d always run it through.

Parkinson’s is my version of a universal condition. Every practitioner has something: attention that fragments under pressure, memory that loses threads, processing that slows with fatigue, language that doesn’t always surface on demand. The biological system we run our judgment through is never perfect. AI, designed well, augments what each of us needs. The discipline is the same regardless of what you’re augmenting: keep the judgment constitutive, or the writing stops being yours.

I started working with AI the way most people do: as a tool. Draft this. Summarize that. Speed up what I was already doing. That lasted six months. Then something shifted. I was in the middle of a complex argument, the kind that used to hold itself together through a long writing session, and I noticed the AI wasn’t helping me execute the thinking. I was thinking through it. My judgment, my pattern authority, my accumulated perspective finding its way forward through an architecture that could hold what my working memory no longer reliably sustained. The argument didn’t happen inside me and get recorded. It happened across both minds.

That was the moment the tool became something else.

Andy Clark and David Chalmers called this the extended mind, proposed as philosophy in 1998, arrived at out of necessity in my case in 2024. They offered a thought experiment. Otto has Alzheimer’s and uses a notebook the way others use biological memory. The conventional view says the notebook is a tool. Clark and Chalmers argue it is part of Otto’s cognitive system, coupled in a direct, here-and-now causal loop. Thinking happens across both. Otto directs his notebook. The notebook does not direct Otto. That asymmetry is everything.

The coupling can build the practitioner or quietly replace them. I developed a test and kept returning to it: is this judgment I earned, or fluency I accepted? It doesn’t catch everything. It catches enough.

That distinction shapes every interaction with AI. Treat AI output as first material, not final material. Use it for structure, contrast, and clarity testing. Use it to find the gaps in your own argument. Do not let it finalize voice. A practitioner who defers judgment to AI one interaction at a time loses the capacity to exercise it independently. The skill erodes quietly, below the threshold of awareness, until the moment it’s needed most.

Augmentation builds the practitioners. Automation replaces them.

What the writer brings

In the first part of this essay, I established where pattern authority comes from. The craft question is how it shows up in the prose.

Practitioner authority rests on consequence-bearing experience, not credential. Academic authority comes from method and institutional affiliation. Thought leadership authority comes from platform size and reputation management. Practitioner authority comes from having been responsible for an outcome, not studying it, not advising on it from a safe distance, but owning what happened next. That weight shows in every sentence or it doesn’t show at all. You can’t install it and you can’t fake it.

This holds whether you write about surgery, software, organizational change, or bridge design. The field is incidental. The relationship to consequence is not.

For consultants the authority takes a different form. Few of us carry direct accountability for outcomes. But years of proximity to consequence, watching patterns across organizations, being trusted with decisions you don’t formally own, learning whose experience to trust and why, builds something real. You know what good judgment looks like under pressure because you’ve watched it fail and succeed across dozens of organizations. That’s not the same as owning the outcome. It’s not nothing either. Earned differently. Still earned.

That different foundation creates a different contract with the reader. Academic-essayistic writing builds the scaffolding first: define, contextualize, qualify, then deploy. Practitioner Voice drops a term into a lived context and trusts the reader to close the gap from their own experience. The scaffolding isn’t missing. The reader is the scaffolding.

Show the scar. The practitioner who has only succeeded has limited range. The one who has failed, learned, and kept going has the full picture. Academic writing contains failure in a limitations section, safely quarantined from the argument. Thought leadership avoids failure entirely; it undermines the brand. Practitioner Voice uses failure as a source of credibility. The scar is the credential. Ground your authority in consequence, not in the degrees on the wall.

Staying visible is harder than it sounds. The framework, the data, the existing literature — these earn their place when they serve your judgment. They become camouflage when they replace it. Your judgment is the point. Stay in the frame.

How the form works

One practical technique before you start: write the back cover first. For a book, this forces three questions before a single chapter exists: who is this for, what will they get from it, and why does it matter now. For an article, write the LinkedIn lede first. Same discipline, different form. If you can’t state the claim in three sentences for a practitioner audience, the piece isn’t ready to draft.

Four principles define how Practitioner Voice works on the page:

Start with the claim. Academic writing earns the conclusion through evidence, argument, and qualification. Practitioner Voice opens with the conclusion and “lets the rest of the piece be explanation, not proof. If the reader has lived the pattern they’ll recognize the claim immediately. If they haven’t, no amount of scaffolding will convince them. Trust the reader to close the gap.

Compression as respect. Write as if the reader already knows more than they can easily articulate. Fewer definitions. Shorter transitions. Declarative statements over explanatory ones. Space between ideas. If something feels obvious to an experienced practitioner, don’t apologize for that; let recognition do the work. Completeness is optional. Resonance is not.

Inspiration and information, blended. Practitioners often write as if these are separate: lead with a story, then deliver the lesson; open with a hook, then provide the data. Practitioner Voice doesn’t separate them. The information arrives inside the inspiration. The insight carries the evidence with it. When it works, the reader doesn’t experience a gear shift from engaging to informative. The piece stays in one register throughout because the judgment and the data are inseparable. If you find yourself writing a section that is purely inspirational or purely informational, that’s the signal. Blend it back.

Consider the tension between Mik Kersten and Jurgen Appelo earlier in this piece. One wrote every word himself; the other co-wrote with a team of AI agents. Both positions are principled. Both carry risk. Naming that tension without collapsing it gives the reader something more useful than either answer alone.

Leaving tension live is harder than it sounds. Name it. Illuminate it. Step back. Do not resolve it for the reader; resolving it would be lying. The tension is real and the reader must navigate it themselves. This is the closing constraint that separates Practitioner Voice from every other professional writing form. Academic writing resolves tension in the conclusion. Thought leadership resolves it in the three takeaways. Practitioner Voice leaves it live because that’s where the judgment lives.

Story: the mechanism that makes ideas move

Facts inform. Arguments persuade. Stories move people to act.

Chip and Dan Heath put it plainly: “A credible idea makes people believe. An emotional idea makes people care. The right story makes people act.” That hierarchy matters for practitioners who write. Most professional writing stops at credible. Practitioner Voice reaches for all three.

Consider the Agile Manifesto, one of the stickiest ideas in software history. The value, “working software over comprehensive documentation”, has been cited, debated, and misapplied for more than twenty years. What made it stick? It was simple without being simplistic, a complex idea in direct language that guides action without prescribing it. It was unexpected; until then, methodologies emphasized architecture and design, and code just followed blueprints. It was concrete; anyone in the software business immediately knows what working software means. It carried credibility from recognized practitioners. It carried emotion for developers exhausted by failing traditional methods.

And it had a story. The Snowbird ski resort. Seventeen people in a room. A manifesto written in two days. That origin narrative has been retold thousands of times. The story of how the idea was born is often stickier than the idea itself.

Practitioners underestimate the power of story. We get tangled in technology and methodology, facts and figures, analysis and concepts. Good ideas get neglected because we fail to engage people emotionally as well as intellectually. A story doesn’t decorate an argument. It is the argument’s delivery mechanism, the thing that makes the reader feel tension before they understand it.

Practitioner Voice is built for this. The scar is a story. The moment of recognition is a story. The project that failed, the client who pushed back, the decision that turned out wrong; these are not digressions from the argument. They are the argument, carried in narrative form. Show the scar is a storytelling instruction as much as a credibility instruction.

Stories don’t have to come from the conference room. A mountaineering moment, a physical consequence, a landscape that forced a decision; these carry the same authority as a project war story, sometimes more. The terrain metaphor earns its place in Practitioner Voice because it connects abstract judgment to embodied experience. Readers who have never managed a software project have still stood at the edge of something uncertain and had to decide.

Craft the story before you craft the argument. Know what happened, who was there, what the stakes were, and what changed. Then build the argument around it. The story is not the illustration. It is the foundation.

Structure: braided narrative

Most professional writing defaults to one of two structures: chronological or logical. Chronological moves through time. Logical moves through argument, problem to solution, claim to evidence. Both are serviceable. Neither is the only option.

The braided narrative weaves multiple threads simultaneously, each developing independently while reinforcing the others. A reader follows several strands at once, and the meaning emerges from their intersection rather than from a single linear argument. The structure is common in literary nonfiction and almost unknown in technical and management writing, which is exactly why it’s worth naming here. It is more difficult to execute than either chronological or logical structure. When it works, it is more rewarding than either.

My Wild West to Agile uses five braids across four eras of software development:

  • The evolution of methods and methodologies
  • Personal experiences and growth across six decades
  • The pioneers who drove each era forward
  • The explosion of technology innovation
  • The progressive management trends that shaped the field

No single braid carries the book. The argument lives in how they weave together.

John Willis’s Rebels of Reason combines braided narrative with chronology: a spine running from Aristotle to ChatGPT with multiple threads running through it, philosophical, technical, and biographical. The chronology orients the reader. The braids create the texture and the surprise.

The braided narrative suits Practitioner Voice because it keeps tension live across multiple dimensions simultaneously. No single thread resolves while the others are still running. The reader holds several things at once, which is closer to how experienced practitioners think than any single-thread argument allows.

When to consider braids: when your subject has more than one dimension that can’t be subordinated to a single argument without losing something essential. When you find yourself writing parallel tracks and forcing them into sequence, that’s the signal. The braids want to run together.

Three levels of editing

The most common editing mistake is fixing the spelling before the argument is worth saving. I once coached a colleague on his first book. He would write a paragraph, then polish it to death before moving to the next. The momentum never built. I kept pushing him to write more and write faster, get the argument down before refining the sentences. It wasn’t his natural style. He resisted, then adapted. The book got finished and published. The polish habit didn’t kill the book. It nearly did.

Mixing levels too early distracts from the work that matters most at each stage. Three levels of editing serve different purposes and need to happen in sequence.

Developmental editing (challenges thinking). It looks at the piece as a whole: purpose, argument, structure, audience, flow, missing ideas, weak logic, and unnecessary material. The goal is to strengthen thinking and architecture before polishing the prose. Claims that may eventually need support should be flagged, but citation mechanics and reference formatting should not derail development before the argument has settled. Key question: does this work as a piece of writing?

Line Editing (improves the writing). It works at paragraph and sentence level to improve clarity, flow, emphasis, voice, rhythm, transitions, word choice, and concision without changing the core argument. Each paragraph should carry a clear idea, develop it coherently, and connect naturally to what comes before and after. Key question: does each paragraph carry one clear idea, and does the language say what I mean in the way I want to say it?

Proofreading (cleans up the writing). It catches grammar, spelling, punctuation, typos, formatting inconsistencies, and other mechanical errors. This is also the right stage for a final check of citations, references, links, and source formatting. Key question: is this clean, correct, and ready to publish?

One rule on citations: identify gaps early, fix mechanics late. The point is not to ignore evidence. It is to keep the reference apparatus from becoming the tail that wags the article. First make sure the argument deserves to survive. Then make the citations impeccable. Citation placement breaks the train of thought at the moment it matters most. Name the source naturally in prose when it’s relevant, put the full reference at the end, and trust the reader to follow up if they want to.

Citations also exist out of respect for other writers. Years ago I was reading an article online. The further I read, the more familiar it felt. I pulled out my Agile Software Development Ecosystems book and found the entire article copied word for word from one of my chapters. No reference. No attribution. That was more than a citation failure. That was plagiarism. Citations exist because ideas belong to people. Put them at the end so they don’t interrupt the reading. But put them in.

Word choice and context calibration

Simple words are not weak words. They are precise words that don’t require the reader to translate. Every technical term should earn its place by doing something a plain word cannot. When a simpler word exists, use it. When the technical term is the right tool, use that. The test is precision, not prestige.

Before you calibrate the vocabulary, identify the reader. Your target audience is narrower than you think. The more precisely you can picture the person reading this, the easier every word choice becomes.

Context calibration is the deeper skill, and it applies to every vocabulary choice a practitioner makes. A cardiologist telling a colleague that a patient presented with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis uses precise shorthand among people trained to receive it. She tells the family the lungs are scarring and breathing will keep getting harder. Same condition, same doctor, same precision, different context. The clinical vocabulary doesn’t disappear. It stays where it belongs. Before reaching for any term, technical or otherwise, the practitioner asks: does this reader share the context that makes this word useful? If yes, use it. If not, translate.

The same discipline applies to consultant vocabulary. “Organizational agility” in a room full of practitioners who live inside that definition is efficient shorthand; everyone knows you mean how fast we can change direction without breaking and saying it the long way wastes their time. The same term dropped into an executive briefing without translation becomes camouflage; it signals tribal membership instead of transferring meaning. The first time you use a term with a mixed audience, define it once in plain language, briefly, then move. After that the shorthand is earned. Context calibration isn’t a prohibition on professional vocabulary. It’s the judgment call that determines when vocabulary serves the reader and when it serves only the writer.

Here is what that looks like in practice. A recent draft contained this sentence: “The contracting model prices the surface and is silent on the substrate, not because the substrate doesn’t matter, but because it was never in the model. It is the same blind spot as your dashboard, in peer-reviewed form.” Correct, precise, and written for an audience that will stop and work through the sentence.

Rewritten for a practitioner: “The contracting model measures what it can see and misses what it can’t. Same blind spot as your dashboard. Just peer-reviewed.” Same idea. One beat of support. Reader closes the gap. That is the difference, and it is not a cosmetic one.

At the sentence level:

  • Use active verbs. Reduce “is” and “was”; build sentences around what things do, not what they are.
  • Minimize gerunds ending in -ing where a direct verb works better.
  • Use “that” sparingly.
  • Plan sentence lengths deliberately; short sentences accelerate, long ones slow the reader down.
  • A period is a stop sign. A colon announces something ahead. A dash is a tree branch in the road. Use each one knowing what it does to the reader’s pace.

Who you write for

Knowing who you write for changes every sentence. Academics write for peer reviewers. Thought leadership writes for eyeballs. Practitioner Voice writes for people who have lived the pattern and will recognize it when someone states it plainly. You are not writing for everyone. You are writing for the reader who has lived this pattern or will. Close enough to recognize it when they do. Far enough out that your experience arrives before theirs does.

Practitioner Voice is comfortable with limited context. This worked here, under these conditions; judge for yourself whether it fits your situation. That’s a different contract with the reader than academic or thought leadership writing offers. Both push toward universal claims: academic writing for impact factor, thought leadership for audience size. Practitioner Voice trusts specificity. A piece that says “here’s what I saw and what I concluded, in this context,” is more honest and often more useful than one dressed up as universal truth.

A piece is as long as the tension requires and no longer. Short is not a virtue; unnecessary length is a failure.

Most pieces earn a carry phrase: a closing line that sticks. Not a summary. A reorientation. The reader finishes thinking: yes, that’s the tension I’ve been living with. Not every structure calls for it. The inverted pyramid lets the reader exit once they have what they need. But when the form allows it, know what line you’re building toward before you write the opening.

The category now has a name. The Practitioner Voice now has craft guidelines. What it still needs is practitioners willing to write this way, to stay in the frame, show the scar, and trust the reader to close the gap.

That part can’t be outlined.

Reactions, pushbacks, and examples from your own practice are welcome. The conversation is on LinkedIn.

It is a discipline: start with the claim, stay visible, ground authority in consequence, compress without losing meaning, and leave real tension live. The goal is not to sound more personal. The goal is to make earned judgment useful to readers who have lived the problem.

Modern software engineering gives us a set of practices that we tend to carry from one project to another: AI assisted development, automated testing, CI/CD, observability, automation, simulation, and safe deployment. They work well enough that we sometimes forget to question the assumptions behind them.

I had to question some of those assumptions when our team started modernizing a large retail IoT system. The system had around 800,000 battery-powered sensors deployed across 3000 stores. The existing connectivity technology was reaching the end of its life, and we needed to move to a newer technology without replacing the installed devices, and also onboard newer stores with next gen devices.

Our team knew software engineering well. We had experience with web applications, cloud platforms, mobile applications, IoT and other distributed systems. What we did not have was deep experience in embedded firmware and large-scale device networks. We thought the software engineering skills would apply here too, and it did, the engineering principles remain the same, but the default practices changed.

Let us find how we discover this change.

Learn by building an experimentation environment

After initial spikes on firmware development technology, our challenge was no more writing the firmware, but actually to understand the IOT system that has been running for years, as the organizational changes had left gaps in the knowledge of the existing firmware, hardware and network architecture.

Documentation helped, but it wasn't enough. Things weren't documented, and some documents described hardware or behaviour we couldn't reproduce. Some answers could only be found by putting our hands on the actual devices, and playing with limited access to production systems.

So we started building things and measuring what actually happened. We built an IoT lab with physical sensors, wire harnesses and learning kits. We created environments where we could experiment with radio behaviour, reused sensors with dead batteries for testing, and measured power consumption and network behaviour.

All these initially looked like our preparation, trials but quickly all this started becoming our engineering work, and soon we were not waiting to understand the system. The IOT lab became part of how we learned, and reverse engineered.

For embedded systems, sometimes the fastest way to answer a question is not to read another document, but to connect the device and see what happens.

Consider the physical world part of the development lifecycle

In conventional software, the development environment is usually made up of software tools. A developer can clone a repository, install dependencies and run the application irrespective of physical location, working from anywhere.

The equivalent setup for our project needed something else. It needed physical devices. We end up creating what we called a sensor farm: a controlled collection of real devices connected to the new network, with monitoring around them. This enabled our engineers to work with multiple devices and observe what happened when they communicated, slept, woke up or lost connectivity. Physical placement, radio conditions and power, all became part of development and testing.

We didn't need every developer to have a laboratory on their desk, but we did need the development process to provide access to the physical behaviour of the system and get fast feedback, the engineering practices like TDD, Automation, XP were all applicable but with hardware in loop.

Every device must be able to explain itself

Once we had a working device, well integrated as part of the development environment, another question appeared: “What happens when the device is somewhere we cannot reach?” This sounds like an operational question, but it turned out to be an architectural one.

Imagine an engineer receives a report that a sensor isn't behaving correctly. The sensor is sitting in a store or development environment, and the engineer is somewhere else. In this case there is no debugger attached, there may be no one available to open the device, the device may be asleep, and the network may not even be available.

A conventional application can often tell us what happened through logs and traces, but a physical device doesn't automatically have that capability. We therefore started building diagnostics into the device firmware itself, where we wanted to know things like which firmware was running, whether the device was healthy, when it last communicated, what its network state was, what happened before a failure, whether it was sleeping, whether it was repeatedly reconnecting, and what its firmware upgrade status was.

We added health checks and diagnostic information, ways to access that information locally, and APIs so that the same information could be retrieved remotely. We then started feeding the information into dashboards and operational tooling.

This changed the way we thought about observability. We weren't simply adding logging to an application. We were designing a system that could operate devices we could not physically see, where each device needed to explain itself. For a small number of devices, this is useful. For hundreds of thousands, it becomes essential.

Design interfaces for engineers as deliberately as interfaces for users.

Diagnostics solved only part of the problem. Engineers also needed ways to interact with the device without physically opening it.

We needed local interfaces such as NFC and BLE, as well as remote interfaces through the gateway and platform. These allowed engineers to inspect configuration, retrieve diagnostics, understand device state and perform operations remotely.

This made us think differently about engineering interfaces. We normally spend a lot of time designing interfaces for users, while interfaces for engineers and operators can become an afterthought.

For a large device fleet, they are part of the system.

Simulate what is expensive to reproduce physically

The next surprise came when we increased the number of devices, and reached the real store.

Everything was fine, until we onboarded a handful of devices, onboarded smaller stores, but as we moved to larger stores, the network infrastructure had limits we had not encountered during smaller lab experiments. At one point, we discovered that the new network hardware could support only a limited number of devices—far below the scale required by some larger stores.

Testing a few devices is very different from testing thousands. Network behavior, infrastructure limits, message rates, device physical location constraints and device disconnection problems started appearing at scales that were difficult to reproduce physically.

So we built a virtual device emulator: special firmware for the same device that could simulate hundreds of unique devices, each can be configured behave differently under different network and environmental conditions. Running many of these virtual devices together allowed us to simulate a large store environment and test the parts of the system where scale itself was the problem. This did not replace physical testing. We still needed real devices to validate firmware, hardware and radio behavior.

We also built a virtual store that behaved like a real store, with a gateway publishing simulated sensor readings to the platform. This allowed us to exercise the downstream systems at store scale without needing hundreds of physical devices for every test.

Design for disconnection, not just connection.

Enterprise applications often make a comfortable assumption: the network is available, and it is considered an infrastructure concern, and applications need to make sure it handles disconnection with a good user-friendly way, letting application reconnect immediately.

A battery-powered device has a different relationship with the network.

The device may sleep on idle to save battery, It may temporarily lose connectivity. It may reconnect repeatedly. It may not be reachable at the exact moment the platform wants to communicate with it. Remember that a connection attempt is the heaviest operation for the device.

We therefore had to carefully design for intermittent connectivity rather than treating it as an exceptional failure. This affected firmware, gateway communication, commands, telemetry and device management. Once we accepted that the device would sometimes be unavailable, many design decisions became clearer.

Treat energy consumption as a software design concern.

There was another constraint that was easy to underestimate: the device had a limited amount of energy, but it is supposed to be operational for years.

In a server application, an inefficient operation might consume more CPU, memory or increase cloud cost. In a battery-powered sensor, unnecessary computation or communication can reduce the useful life of the device.

We introduced power measurement and profiling into our development process. We looked at when the device was awake, how often it communicated and what different operations meant for battery consumption.

The important thing wasn't simply optimizing the code. It was understanding that every design decision could have a physical consequence—even something as small as a log statement or a few lines of code that appeared to be unused.

We also had to rethink some of our usual assumptions about memory management. Instead of aggressively cleaning up allocated memory after every operation, in some cases we chose a simpler approach: let the device run for 24 hours and then reboot it as part of its normal operating cycle.

On a device, sometimes the simplest software solution is not the one we would choose in a server.

Design deployment and recovery together.

Firmware deployment introduced another challenge.

A cloud application can often be rolled back quickly when something goes wrong. Physical devices distributed across thousands of stores does not give us that luxury.

The battery consumed in downloading and installing firmware can not be rolled back. The device might be offline during an update. The network might fail halfway through a download. The firmware might not validate correctly. Or a problem might only become visible after deployment. All this would change the meaning of deployment and recovery.

We therefore designed firmware updates with recovery as part of the deployment mechanism. We implemented over the air firmware updates using secure downloads, validation and partition swapping. Updates could be applied to individual devices, groups of devices or stores, with progress visible through the gateway and, where useful, locally through NFC. The device also stored its firmware upgrade state, allowing an update to resume from where it left off after recovering from an interruption or failure.

More importantly, we designed a staged rollout, as we wanted to know what happened after an update before updating everything. After all, the question was no longer just, “How do we deploy the new firmware?” but, “How do we deploy it safely, and what happens when it goes wrong?”

Optimize the engineering process for confidence at scale.

By this point, something subtle had changed.

Early in the project, we talked like software engineers. How quickly can we build this? How quickly can we deploy it? How automated can we make the pipeline?

Those questions still mattered. But increasingly, our conversations became different. Can we trust this firmware update? Can we recover if something goes wrong? Can we explain why this device failed? Can we understand what is happening across a store? Can we safely update thousands of devices? What will this do to battery life? And how long will it take to upgrade a store?

We were optimizing for something slightly different: confidence. That didn't mean giving up speed. It meant recognizing that speed without confidence isn't necessarily progress. For a physical fleet, a fast deployment that creates thousands of unhealthy devices is a very efficient way to create a large problem.

Design observability for the fleet, not just the device.

Making an individual device explain itself was necessary, but it was not sufficient. With hundreds of thousands of devices, nobody can inspect them one by one. The question changed from “What is this device doing?” to “What is happening across the fleet?”

We built dashboards and analytics to identify communication failures, unusual behavior, outages, firmware distribution, patterns and other fleet-level conditions. Operational teams needed alerts and tools that could show whether a problem was isolated or affecting a much larger part of the fleet.

The engineering environment became part of the system

By this point, several things that had started as engineering or operational tools had become essential parts of the overall system.

The physical sensor farm helped us learn and test. The virtual device emulator helped us test at scale. Diagnostic interfaces allowed engineers to understand devices remotely. The gateway provided communication and management capabilities. Dashboards and analytics allowed operations teams to understand the fleet.

The architecture started looking something like this:

Device → Firmware, Diagnostics and Configuration → IoT Gateway → Telemetry, Commands and OTA → Fleet Platform → Analytics, Alerts and Operations

Figure 1: An engineering environment: Hardware, Software, and Feedback

These were not simply developer conveniences. Together they allowed us to build, test, operate, migrate and manage a very large physical fleet. The more devices we had, the more valuable this surrounding platform became.

Use AI to shorten the learning loop, not just the coding loop.

AI also became part of how we worked, although not in the way we initially expected.

We used LLMs to explore unfamiliar areas, prototype solutions and shorten the time between a question and a useful experiment. We also used AI-assisted development to build dashboards, migration trackers, outage detection and other engineering tools more quickly.

The important benefit was not simply generating code. It was reducing the cost of trying something.

Capture discoveries, not just decisions.

We were learning through experiments, failures, measurements and operational incidents. If we did not capture those discoveries, the next person would have to learn the same lesson again.

Documentation therefore became more than recording architecture decisions. We captured what we had learned about devices, networks, testing, diagnostics, deployment and operations, and shared that learning through technical articles, training and our engineering community.

Traditional documentation often tells us what the system is. In an unfamiliar domain, it is equally valuable to capture how we discovered why it is that way.

The principles stayed, the defaults changed

Looking back, I don't think we invented a new methodology for IoT or embedded software.

We still wanted fast feedback, automation, good testing, observability, maintainability, safe deployment and continuous learning. What changed was how those principles were practiced.

Over time, the changes looked like a new set of defaults.

We started with this assumptionWe ended up with this sensible defaultDocumentation should tell us enoughLearn by building an experimentation environmentHardware can be tested laterConsider the physical world part of the development lifecycleA device performs its function, and platform can always explain its healthEvery device must be able to explain itselfInterfaces are primarily for usersDesign interfaces for engineers as deliberately as interfaces for usersNetwork behavior, physical environment can be tested and reproduced with a few devices in labSimulate what is expensive to reproduce physicallyDevices should normally be reachableDesign for disconnection, not just connectionBattery is mainly a hardware concernTreat energy consumption as a software design concernDeployment means installing firmwareDesign deployment and recovery togetherOptimize primarily for delivery speedOptimize the engineering process for confidence at scaleObservability means logs and metricsDesign observability for the fleet, not just the deviceBuild the product, then supporting toolsThe engineering environment became part of the systemAI helps write codeUse AI to shorten the learning loop, not just the coding loopDiscovery happens before development and capture decisions in the final designCapture discoveries, not just decisions

The table is a record of what happened. Each default was earned by encountering a problem.

Why call them sensible defaults?

I use the term sensible defaults deliberately.

None of these practices was invented from first principles. Most emerged from problems we encountered. We started with an assumption that seemed reasonable, ran into something that challenged it, experimented, and gradually changed the way we worked.

That is how engineering practices often evolve in real projects. The environment tells you where your assumptions are wrong. If you pay attention, those failures can help you discover a better default.

That was certainly our experience. When software meets hardware, the engineering principles do not necessarily change. But the sensible defaults might.

LLM Voice

29 October 2026

Martin Fowler

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves.

1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up.

2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source).

Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3. Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.

3: Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.”

1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up.

2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source).

I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code. Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut.

In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation:

Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts.

One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at

having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed.

She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data.

Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier.

The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug.

The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control

A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments.

With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses.

The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution.

Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies.

This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans.

A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent

Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on.

And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent

In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to

While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks.

Annie Vella observes that the change we’re seeing in software development follows a way of thinking about automation that goes back to the 1960’s as the distinction between direct and supervisory control.

The main difference between direct and supervisory control is that in the latter, there’s a computer that closes the loop instead of a human operator. Before AI, writing software was much more like direct control - we closed the loop ourselves. We interpreted requirements, made changes to the code, received feedback and acted on it, over and over. Now, coding agents can increasingly close that loop themselves - writing code, running tests and fixing their own mistakes - while we move towards supervisory control: telling the agent what we want, keeping an eye on how it’s going and taking over when we need to.

She outlines various ideas that this intellectual thread developed. The five-level model developed by Endsley and Kiris seems apposite:

LevelHumanSystemIn AI-assisted software development1. NoneDecide, act-No AI assistance2. Decision supportDecide, actSuggestThe early days of AI coding assistants’ autocomplete3. Consensual AIConcurDecide, actAI coding agents where you must approve the actions they take4. Monitored AIVetoDecide, actAuto-mode, with the ability to veto the coding agent’s actions5. Full automation-Decide, actFull auto-mode, such as might be used in a dark software factory

Vella cautions that this comes with an important caveat:

There is one notable difference between the automation described by this prior research and the type of automation that AI agents give us. Both sets of levels assume that the computer’s account of what it did is accurate and honest. As we all know by now, what an AI agent says it did and what it actually did may not be the same thing. Still, it’s automation, and it still requires supervision - arguably more, since we can’t simply take its word for it.

Vella’s conclusion from all this is that: “our next step must be to start redesigning the job and the system, in tandem”. What if we stopped thinking of the SDLC as a process we follow, and instead started thinking of it as a control system we build and supervise?

He opens by looking at our future, saying that rather than fruitlessly trying to predict it, we should instead explore it with “curiosity, fun, and wonder”. He’s been doing this, digging deeper into the theory and fundamentals that underpin AI.

He goes into detail on his side project: the Domain Language Surveyor. The idea is to be able to examine different repositories, and analyze the vocabulary used inside those repositories to see if they are related bounded contexts. To do this he built a pipeline of tools, illustrating how a useful system blends both computational and inferential components. He then used this pipeline to analyze the vocabulary of some open-source healthcare codebases, to see how their bounded contexts related.

A topic that regularly comes up when I talk to companies outside the Foocamp world, is the cost of tokens, and the concern about how that cost is going to increase in the future. We’ve been worrying about that at Thoughtworks, and my colleague Andy Nolan describes our token sourcing strategy, which we forecast will reduce our token costs in 2028 from $16-40M down to $6.8-1M.

The strategy rents frontier models for the work that needs frontier-level reasoning. It runs open-weight models, on capacity we choose, for the work that carries our IP or runs at a volume where owning the capacity costs less.

The strategy involves looking at each LLM workload, and classifying it on two axes: domain differentiation and security & sovereignty. We then place each workload on a nine cell grid.

The nine cells run from the cheapest capable API, swapped as prices change, to a fine-tuned open model on our own infrastructure, with full control and full upkeep. For a given workload, the highest score on a given axis determines the right position in the grid. There is no single right place for all workloads. Each organization ends up with its own distribution and mix of workloads across the grid.

TL;DR
Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production.

I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance?

The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is.

Building it right

Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right. It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right.

Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on.

Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet.

After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect.

And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own.

A week at the whiteboard

Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here.

What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day.

The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team.

When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story…

The application ran. The build was red.

The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it. If it’s red so often that people stop paying attention, how do we spot the next real failure? And if we can’t trust the checks, a green build stops being reassuring too. That’s exactly the uncertainty continuous integration was supposed to remove, and we’ve been advocating it for over 25 years.

We’re still working through how to address it. Remember this was an experiment to push the very edge of agentic development. Were too many agents working in parallel and stepping on each other’s changes? Was the system not yet modular enough for agents to work on separate parts? Or were changes simply arriving faster than the checks could finish? Or was it a combination of all of these and more? Either way we definitely need to rethink how we will solve the last mile challenges. I can see continuous delivery/DevOps as a movement having a resurgence and a rethink in the agentic era in the same way the rest of the development life cycle is being upended. And it isn’t just our experiment. DORA’s 2025 research found AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, but to lower delivery stability. Exactly what continuous delivery and DevOps were trying to solve for!

All of these challenges prompted some good arguments internally. What role should test-driven development play when you aren’t reading every line and the agent created the tests alongside the code? Where would acceptance tests, contract tests and checks at system boundaries give us more confidence without being too brittle? How much design should we do before setting an agent loose, given how quickly we can revise an approach? Is there an appropriate point we will know we have gone too far? One of the biggest puzzles in all this is the size of the batch. I have heard many teams are moving from Stories to Epics. Great for speed of development but can your CI pipeline handle that size unit of work at speed and in parallel?

The experiment team didn’t settle all of this in a week or even two (they ran it twice with different teams). I wouldn’t trust anyone who claimed they had. But this is exactly the kind of work I want experienced developers involved in: experimenting, questioning and helping us discover which practices hold up and where we need some new ones.

Off the groomed slopes

After coming away from this conversation with some of the senior developers involved I kept thinking about learning to ski. Kids will often head straight down the hill without fear, kind of like a new builder who has never put software into production and has never fixed an on-call issue at 3am (something I will never forget, right up there with every production issue I personally caused and the resultant learnings from those, which are burned in my brain forever). When I first tried to ski as an adult, I was thinking about what I might break. I wanted to ski, it looked so fun and freeing, but I was old enough to see the consequences and I didn’t fancy hobbling around London with a broken limb or worse. My biggest issue was I hadn’t yet learned how to turn or stop effectively and without that I was a runaway train on a ski slope.

When I shared a draft of this post with Martin, who also learned to ski late, he pointed out where the comparison breaks down (like all analogies I like to push them to the edge, pun intended). On a ski slope you’ve watched countless people reach the bottom with no broken bones. The instructors have taught thousands of people before you on the same slope. They know which skills matter and how to teach them. Agentic development right now is more like a backcountry trip across unknown territory. We don’t yet know which skills will matter most. Not many people, if any, have finished the trip safely and the feedback on how to navigate it is slow or non-existent. As Martin put it, we won’t know whether a heavily agent-built system works until it has run in production for a while, survived a few rounds of change, and not sent all our planes to Aberystwyth. Built is not the same as working in production. Or as Charity Majors puts it, “staging is just a glorified laptop. Only prod is prod”. Which is why when someone says “it works on my machine” it’s usually intended as a joke. Or at least I always laugh.

That solidified a nagging discomfort I have had with leaders, technical or non-technical, claiming devs aren’t curious, or are laggards slow to adopt, and putting that down to easy-to-point-at fears like missing writing code (I do too) and fearing for our jobs (who isn’t right now?). Our best developers aren’t nervous beginners on a nursery slope that everyone else has already mastered. They’re looking at unmarked terrain and asking sensible questions about the route. Telling them to be less cautious misses the point. They need to be on the team that maps it.

Of course, experience can also make us too attached to familiar practices. Some of what we learned on the groomed slopes won’t hold out there, and we need to be willing to test our assumptions.

A challenge for both sides

So there’s a challenge here for both leaders and developers. Leaders need to listen carefully enough to tell useful concerns from reluctance to change, and to create real room for experimentation. That means time, permission to get things wrong, and not judging success by how much code the agents produced. Developers need to bring their experience into those experiments and be prepared to find that some of their assumptions no longer hold.

Some familiar practices will become more important. Others will need a different shape. Nobody is going to hand us a map first.

If you care deeply about building the right thing and building it right, your judgment is exactly what this new way of working needs. Bring the caution. Then let’s set off into the snow.

Two-thirds of the companies on the Forbes AI 50 list now use some form of usage-based pricing, reflecting AI’s variable costs and unpredictable demand. At the second annual Monetize conference last month, Metronome CEO and Cofounder Scott Woody put it more bluntly: today’s leading companies operate in ways that would seem “alien” to traditional SaaS businesses. These companies are iterating much faster on pricing, prioritizing market share over ARR, and pursuing multiple go-to-market strategies at once.

More than 300 leaders from fast-moving companies like Replit, Fin, Snowflake, and Clay came together at Monetize to trade notes on pricing, cost management, and scaling AI products as customer expectations change. Across sessions, five approaches for how companies are now approaching the economics of AI monetization came up repeatedly.

Hybrid pricing: Packaging usage with subscriptions and credits

A year ago, it was common to expect usage-based pricing to displace subscriptions. Businesses are still using them, just in a new way.We’re seeing more companies using subscriptions to package up variable usage, often through credits.

Aisling O’Reilly, Fin’s director of product for monetization, described the evolution of her own company’s pricing models. The company evolved from a platform subscription to a hybrid model, introducing outcome-based pricing when it launched Fin AI Agent. Initially, customers paid for each support conversation resolved by the agent. As the product expanded into actions like recommending products, qualifying leads, and booking meetings, its original (and only) billable metric became an insufficient representation of customer value. Fin introduced additional billable outcomes, letting customers choose the outcome they wanted from each conversation type and pay based on its value. Customers can commit to a pool of credits, then draw down against that pool across outcomes without having to forecast each one separately.

What’s emerging for Fin and many other companies is a layered model, with subscriptions for actions and predictability, usage-based pricing for agentic work, and credits to simplify multiple usage or outcome units.

Predictability is becoming a product feature

One of the biggest challenges with usage-based billing is giving customers more predictable costs. They need to understand what drives usage, anticipate spend, set spend limits, and connect usage to value. Many companies have addressed those requirements through in-product dashboards, predictions, and other types of tooling.

Snowflake Senior Director Ryan Campbell explained how he and his team help customers monitor and control their consumption through in-product tooling like forecasting, calculators, scenario builders, and usage visibility. Similarly, Stripe’s Head of Global Pricing and Commercialization, Sam Lee, described the usage control pane, where users can see alerts, set and adjust spending controls, and manage consumption, as a new standard.

Commercial terms can also offer more predictability while keeping charges tied to usage. Annual usage buckets, discounted overages, and first-year fixed contracts with follow-on true-ups all offer customers clearer controls to manage variable bills.

As bills become more unpredictable, strong usage controls become part of what customers are paying for. Those controls help build trust in both the company and the product.

Falling AI costs and rising usage call for flexible packaging

With advances in AI, companies are able to package the same product in different ways. Subscriptions can house lower-cost and rate-limited experiences, while usage-based billing can be used for more resource-intensive agent work. Replit uses both as model costs and agent workloads shift, said Michele Catasta, the company’s president and head of AI.

When Replit’s agents used to run for just a few minutes, the company charged 25¢ per agent checkpoint. But as runtimes grew, some jobs cost Replit several dollars while users still paid just 25¢. The company adopted usage-based billing to close the gap, aligning prices more closely with the amount of work performed by its agents.

This move solved one problem and introduced another: unpredictable spending and abrupt paywalls for users accustomed to a straightforward monthly subscription. As inference costs fell—due in part to increasingly capable open-source models and the pressure they put on frontier-model prices—Replit introduced a rate-limited Free Mode. This gives users the ability to keep building on a simple subscription. The company changes elements of its pricing several times a month, passing savings on to customers.

This opens up more flexible packaging beyond the one-product, one-pricing-model approach. Companies can combine subscriptions and usage-based billing, then adjust the mix as the underlying economics shift. That lets them offer versions of the same product at different speeds, prices, and service levels.

Finance’s new mandate: Proving AI value

While tokens might determine a company’s costs, it’s rare that they represent the value customers think they’re buying. In a session on how finance teams can measure AI’s value, Karan Parekh, Clay’s head of finance, said the company doesn’t want to be in the business of “upcharging and taxing tokens.” When pricing, Clay treats model tokens and third-party data as pass-through inputs, separate from the differentiated value its product provides.

Clay applies the same approach to evaluate its own internal AI investments. The sales team tracks productivity, the product team focuses on development time, and support teams measure throughput and customer satisfaction. Parekh’s team is comfortable with its own AI spending growing faster than revenue only if it’s producing something distinctive Clay couldn’t otherwise achieve.

Attribution is difficult when multiple tools and workflow changes contribute to the same result, making token-level ROI calculations misleading. Clay’s solution is to measure AI tooling against those function-specific targets, reviewing them quarterly to track whether those AI investments prove out. For finance teams, operational outcomes are a more useful lens than focusing on input costs.

Pricing information needs to be readable by both machines and humans

Agents are already influencing how products are discovered and evaluated, even if autonomous enterprise purchasing has yet to fully emerge.

To understand how buyers might encounter pricing in AI-generated answers, Kyle Poyar, founder of Growth Unhinged, tested how six AI engines presented pricing information for companies on the Cloud 100. He analyzed 7,600 AI-generated responses. For one unnamed company, negative pricing language appeared in 88% of responses. Without accessible pricing for this organization, LLMs resorted to scouring informal sources like Reddit and reported back prices ranging from $100–$2,400 per user, per month, a 24x difference.

Pricing information might be fully visible to humans who visit your site, but if it’s blocked from crawlers or rendered in a way agents can’t reliably interpret, it’s basically invisible. While autonomous enterprise procurement is still early, pricing now has two different audiences to serve. The person accountable for the purchase is still in the picture, but they’ve made room for the machine helping them evaluate the purchase.

AI monetization is becoming an adaptive system

AI products, model economics, and usage patterns are changing far too quickly for pricing to stay static. Across sessions, leaders described identifying what customers value, giving them more control over spending, and adjusting pricing and packaging as products and business economics change.

Watch the recorded sessions from Monetize 2026 for the full conversations with leaders from Replit, Fin, Snowflake, Clay, Growth Unhinged, and Stripe.

Sync Stripe data directly to Postgres
